scope: Editorial orientation using the existing cited study records; interpretation remains distinct from documentary identification. Not a new universal account or independent specialist review.

leonardo-01.heading: A portrait with an uncertain expression
leonardo-01.subject: A likeness can identify its sitter without documenting what she was feeling. Follow the folded hands and the transition around the mouth before making the expression into a narrative.
leonardo-01.encounter: The panel’s small recorded dimensions and its densely layered history matter alongside its modern celebrity. A screen enlargement changes access to the image, not the physical scale of the object.

leonardo-02.heading: A sacred meal in a room for meals
leonardo-02.subject: The subject is Christ’s announcement of betrayal during the Last Supper. The responses of the apostles distribute a single narrative moment across several groups rather than illustrating twelve identical reactions.
leonardo-02.encounter: A wall painting in a refectory addresses bodies sharing a dining space. Its later survival as a fragile surface, and its reproduction as a portable image, are different conditions of encounter.

rembrandt-01.heading: A commissioned group, not an anonymous crowd
rembrandt-01.subject: A civic company has to be recognizable as a body of people while remaining a composition in movement. Named officers, collective identity and unequal illumination are connected questions, not interchangeable ones.
rembrandt-01.encounter: The present rectangle is a trimmed object. An early copy supports discussion of lost margins; it cannot supply Rembrandt’s exact original colors, touch or every missing material detail.

vermeer-01.heading: A face without an established sitter’s story
vermeer-01.subject: A tronie explores a type, expression or costume without necessarily recording a named sitter’s commissioned likeness. The turned head can create a sense of response without proving a particular relationship to the spectator.
vermeer-01.encounter: Distinguish the modern auction and bequest record from the painting’s undocumented earlier life. Neither the familiar title nor a luminous painted earring establishes an otherwise unknown biography.

van-gogh-01.heading: A night built from different kinds of movement
van-gogh-01.subject: The village supplies recognizable structures while the sky is organized by sweeping rhythms. Describing those differences is more precise than treating every mark as the direct transcription of a mood.
van-gogh-01.encounter: A reproduction shows directed paint marks, but changes in light across the original relief require a material encounter. The recorded setting of the artist’s work does not make the canvas a clinical document.

leonardo-06.heading: A sitter presented through more than a face
leonardo-06.subject: The face, juniper and surviving reverse belong to a portrait with social claims. An interpretation of reserve can describe the spectator’s encounter without claiming access to Ginevra’s private temperament.
leonardo-06.encounter: The panel was cut down. The surviving boundary must not be used as conclusive evidence of the original framing, and a proposed patron or occasion must retain the qualification given by the institution.

michelangelo-02.heading: A biblical subject carried by an interval
michelangelo-02.subject: The encounter represents the creation of Adam. The near contact of the hands organizes attention, but its force depends on the different weights, postures and directions of the larger bodies.
michelangelo-02.encounter: A ceiling image addresses a viewer from below and at a distance. A fitted reproduction allows a close inspection that does not recreate its architectural position or its surrounding narrative program.

raphael-01.heading: Philosophy staged as a shared space
raphael-01.subject: The School of Athens gathers thinkers within an imagined architectural setting. Centrality and gesture organize differences among them; recognizing famous names should lead back to how the gathering is made visible.
raphael-01.encounter: An architectural fresco is not a portable gathering of portraits. Its wall, neighboring images and learned audience contribute to the encounter; identifications of individual figures do not all have the same evidential security.

caravaggio-02.heading: Recognition at the supper table
caravaggio-02.subject: The Emmaus story concerns the recognition of the risen Christ during a meal. Hands, light and projecting objects turn recognition into a bodily encounter rather than a statement that could be read apart from the picture.
caravaggio-02.encounter: This is the London painting, not the later Milan treatment. Comparing versions is useful only after preserving their separate dates, objects and histories.

rembrandt-02.heading: Knowledge performed before an audience
rembrandt-02.subject: The scene presents an anatomical demonstration as well as a professional group. The demonstrator’s hand, the examined body and the gathered faces divide the act of knowing into different visible roles.
rembrandt-02.encounter: A named subject is also a body represented within a professional ceremony. The group’s status and the sitter’s individual identification require historical records; illumination by itself cannot prove consent or private attitudes.

vermeer-05.heading: A balance and a judgment pictured behind it
vermeer-05.subject: The visible arrangement includes a suspended balance, valuables and a Last Judgment image. Those relationships support moral readings, but the woman’s thought is not directly available to the spectator.
vermeer-05.encounter: Keep separate the objects that can be located, the picture-within-the-picture that can be identified, and the argument made from their relation. An interpretation becomes stronger when each step can be examined.

gentileschi-02.heading: An artist and the personification of Painting
gentileschi-02.subject: Self-representation meets allegory: a working body can also carry the attributes of Painting. The identification asks how professional authorship is made visible rather than merely whether the face resembles its maker.
gentileschi-02.encounter: The named allegorical tradition supplies context; the turning body and working arm give the image its particular force. Neither dimension should erase the other.

goya-01.heading: A historical event and a later image of it
goya-01.subject: The execution scene represents violence associated with 1808, in a painting made in 1814. Separating event and execution dates prevents the picture from being treated as an immediate eyewitness photograph.
goya-01.encounter: The alignment of weapons and the differing exposed bodies support an account of organized force. An individual expression remains painted evidence of a represented action, not an independently documented final thought.

turner-01.heading: An event date inside a painting’s title
turner-01.subject: The title’s 1838 belongs to the ship’s final journey; the painting was exhibited in 1839. A title can name historical circumstances without giving the date at which its image was made.
turner-01.encounter: Look at the relation between sailing ship and tug before deciding whether the work simply celebrates progress or laments the past. Its later popularity belongs to reception, not proof of one original response.

monet-02.heading: A figure encountered through changing light
monet-02.subject: The parasol, dress, grass and clouds hold together different degrees of solidity. A recognizable figure gives the eye an anchor while the surrounding handling makes visibility less settled.
monet-02.encounter: Dress and leisure locate a social encounter, but a pleasant setting does not explain away the painterly work. Compare where a contour remains firm with where adjacent colors carry the form.

morisot-02.heading: A boat whose frame opens beyond the picture
morisot-02.subject: The figures occupy a close, partly cropped boat on reflective water. The scene can sustain questions about companionship and spectator position without assigning a documented conversation to its occupants.
morisot-02.encounter: The date is approximate: About 1879. The later Lane credit belongs to collection history, not the moment of execution, and the outing’s subject does not prove that every part was painted outdoors.

cassatt-01.heading: Care organized through touch and pattern
cassatt-01.subject: The adult and child are joined through hands, feet and the basin. Repeated patterns and the downward viewpoint make care a spatial arrangement as well as a represented activity.
cassatt-01.encounter: A painted maternal relationship is not automatically the artist’s autobiography. Models, posing and composition belong to making; the later purchase record belongs to the object’s institutional life.

van-gogh-02.heading: Labor represented, and labor described by the artist
van-gogh-02.subject: The meal, working hands and shared light can be examined in the image. Van Gogh’s letter explains what he wanted the picture to communicate; it does not supply an independent account of the models’ own experience.
van-gogh-02.encounter: The letter, the canvas and the related lithograph are different kinds of evidence. Their connection should not be turned into an invented sequence of studies or an assumption that all versions show identical arrangements.

kandinsky-02.heading: Relationships without a single represented scene
kandinsky-02.subject: Circles, lines and angular forms distribute visual weight without requiring one named landscape or event. The question is how their differences organize attention, not which hidden object unlocks every shape.
kandinsky-02.encounter: Geometric clarity in a reproduction does not make the painting a technical diagram. An account of rhythm or balance is an editorial reading to test against the particular arrangement.

cezanne-01.heading: A still life whose supports will not settle
cezanne-01.subject: Apples, a tilted bottle, cloth and a basket make a recognizable arrangement whose alignments are difficult to reconcile. The objects remain substantial while the support that seems to hold them becomes uncertain.
cezanne-01.encounter: The painting asks how a table can be convincing without behaving like a single measured plane. That spatial reading describes visible relationships; it does not establish an unrecorded sequence of sittings or a particular private intention.
